blocks.content: Every topic in this course so far, processes, scheduling, memory management, has lived inside RAM. The moment the power goes off, all of that state disappears. This module shifts focus to a different problem entirely: how does a computer keep data around permanently. The answer is the file system, the part of the operating system responsible for organizing, naming, storing, and retrieving data on non-volatile storage so it survives reboots, crashes, and power loss.

This chapter is the opening topic of that module, File Systems and Storage. It lays the conceptual foundation that every later topic in the module builds on: what a file system actually is, why an operating system needs one at all, what a file consists of underneath, and how this whole abstraction connects to the physical hardware it ultimately sits on.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409066980-719601745.png
1. What a File System Is and Why We Need One
blocks.text: 1. What a File System Is and Why We Need One

blocks.content: A raw disk, whether it is a spinning hard drive or a solid state drive, is nothing more than an enormous flat array of numbered blocks. Block 0, block 1, block 2, all the way up to however many blocks the device holds. There is no concept of a file name, no folders, no permissions, nothing that resembles the files and folders you interact with every day. If an application had to work directly with raw block numbers, it would need to remember that its data lives in blocks 4102 through 4198, and it would have no clean way to ask for more space or to safely share that data with another program.

A file system is the layer of abstraction that turns that raw block array into the familiar world of files and folders that users and programs actually interact with. It sits between applications and the physical storage device, translating human friendly operations like create this file or open that folder into the low level block reads and writes the hardware understands. Everything from a text document to a video to an entire application is, underneath, just a name the file system maps onto a set of disk blocks.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409067608-845228978.png
blocks.alt: What a File System Is and Why We Need One

blocks.content: A file system exists to turn an enormous flat array of numbered disk blocks into the files and folders every user and program actually understands.

blocks.title: Why not just use raw blocks
blocks.content: Working with raw block numbers directly would be like navigating a city using only GPS coordinates, with no street names, no addresses, and no signposts. The file system is what gives storage the equivalent of streets, addresses, and directions.
2. The Core Responsibilities of a File System
blocks.text: 2. The Core Responsibilities of a File System

blocks.content: A file system carries out several distinct jobs at once, and each one solves a real problem that would exist if raw disks were used directly. Understanding these responsibilities individually makes the rest of this module far easier to follow, because nearly every later topic in the module is really a deep dive into one of them.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409067610-910898630.png
blocks.alt: The Core Responsibilities of a File System

blocks.content: Naming

A file system gives every piece of data a human meaningful name, such as resume.pdf or budget.xlsx, instead of forcing users and programs to refer to it by raw block numbers. Names can be typed, remembered, and searched for by a person, which raw disk addresses never could be.
Organizing

Files rarely exist in isolation, so a file system arranges them into a navigable hierarchy of directories, commonly called folders. This hierarchy is what lets you nest a project folder inside a documents folder inside your home folder, and it is a rich enough topic on its own that the sibling Directory Structure topic in this module covers it in full.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409067611-797752618.png
Storage allocation

Somewhere underneath the names and folders, the file system has to decide exactly which physical disk blocks belong to which file, and keep that mapping consistent as files grow, shrink, and get deleted. Different file systems make very different tradeoffs here, and that comparison is exactly what the sibling File Allocation Methods topic in this module explores in depth.
Access control

Not every user or program should be able to read, write, or execute every file. The file system stores permissions alongside each file and enforces them on every access attempt, which is what stops one user's files from being casually read or modified by another user or a misbehaving program.
Metadata tracking

Alongside a file's actual content, the file system tracks a whole set of descriptive information: its size, when it was created and last modified, who owns it, and what permissions apply to it. Crucially, this metadata is stored separately from the file's content, an idea the next section covers directly and the sibling Inodes topic goes much deeper into.
3. What a File Actually Consists Of: Data and Metadata
blocks.text: 3. What a File Actually Consists Of: Data and Metadata

blocks.content: From the operating system's point of view, every file is really two related but separate things. The first is the file's data, the actual bytes of content, the words in a document, the pixels in an image, the instructions in a program. The second is the file's metadata, information that describes the file without being part of its content.

Metadata typically includes the file's size, its creation and last modified timestamps, its owner, its permissions, and critically, a pointer to where its actual data blocks live on disk. This separation matters in practice more than it might seem. It is why an operating system can rename a file instantly without touching a single byte of its content, and why it can list a folder's contents almost instantly without reading the actual data inside every file, since it only has to read the much smaller metadata.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409067612-542124472.png
blocks.alt: What a File Actually Consists Of: Data and Metadata

blocks.title: A common misconception
blocks.content: It is tempting to think of a file as just its raw bytes and nothing else. In reality, the metadata describing a file, its name, size, timestamps, owner, and permissions, is just as essential a part of what a file is as its content, and the operating system stores the two separately.
4. File Operations and File Attributes

Every interaction a program has with a file eventually reduces to a small set of operations: create, open, read, write, close, and delete. Together these form the full lifecycle of a file, from the moment it comes into existence to the moment it is removed. The sibling File Operations topic in this module covers this lifecycle and the exact system call sequence behind each step in full depth, so this chapter only introduces the idea in passing.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409067612-801253146.png

Separately from the operations you can perform on a file, every file also carries a fixed set of attributes describing what it is. These attributes are what a file manager or a command like ls or dir is actually displaying when it lists a folder, and they are drawn directly from the file's metadata described above.

5. A File System as a Pluggable Abstraction
blocks.text: 5. A File System as a Pluggable Abstraction

blocks.content: There is not just one file system in the world, there are many: FAT32, NTFS, ext4, APFS, and others. Each is a different concrete implementation of the same underlying idea, and each makes different tradeoffs in areas like maximum file size, performance, journaling support, and compatibility across operating systems.

What makes this workable is a classic and important separation in operating system design: applications above the file system layer do not need to know or care which concrete file system is underneath. Whether a USB drive is formatted with FAT32, a Windows disk with NTFS, a Linux disk with ext4, or a Mac SSD with APFS, an application still just calls the same create, open, read, write, and delete operations. The file system abstraction is the interface, and the specific implementation underneath is free to vary.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409067612-686872948.png
blocks.alt: A File System as a Pluggable Abstraction

6. Worked Example: Saving a New Text File
blocks.text: 6. Worked Example: Saving a New Text File

blocks.content: Tracing through a single concrete example ties the ideas above together. Suppose a user opens a text editor, types a short note, and clicks Save, giving the file the name notes.txt.

Conceptually, the file system layer does four things in sequence. It allocates free disk blocks large enough to hold the new data. It creates a metadata entry recording the file's name, size, timestamp, and permissions. It registers that new entry in the appropriate directory, so the file becomes visible when that folder is listed. Finally, it returns a reference the application can use for any further reads or writes.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409067613-536344638.png
blocks.alt: Worked Example: Saving a New Text File

blocks.title: Kept intentionally high level
blocks.content: The exact mechanics behind each of these four steps, how free blocks are found, how metadata is actually laid out, how directory entries are structured, belong to the sibling Inodes, File Allocation Methods, and Directory Structure topics. This walkthrough is deliberately kept conceptual.
7. Why File Systems Matter, and What Comes Next
blocks.text: 7. Why File Systems Matter, and What Comes Next

blocks.content: File systems matter enormously in the real world, well beyond just letting you double click an icon. A poorly designed or poorly implemented file system can lose data during a crash, fragment storage until performance degrades, or fail to scale to the file counts and sizes modern applications demand. A well designed one can survive power loss mid write, serve millions of small files efficiently, and squeeze meaningfully more throughput out of the exact same physical hardware.

This topic has only laid the groundwork. The rest of this module builds directly on top of it: how directories are structured internally, how inodes track file metadata precisely, how blocks get allocated to files under different allocation strategies, how journaling protects a file system against crashes mid write, how disk scheduling orders physical reads and writes for performance, and finally how the underlying hardware itself, SSD versus HDD, and RAID, shapes everything above it.

9. Interview Angle

In an interview setting, be ready to state clearly, in a sentence or two, what the core responsibilities of a file system are: naming, organizing, storage allocation, access control, and metadata tracking. Interviewers often follow up by asking you to explain the difference between a file's data and its metadata, since that distinction underlies almost every later topic in this module, from inodes to journaling.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.content: If asked to define a file system in one sentence, something like this works well: a file system is the operating system subsystem that organizes, names, stores and retrieves data on non-volatile storage, and separates a file's descriptive metadata from its actual content.
